thread.title: American Public Education: Short This Stock As Students Close The Books On Formal Education - American Public Education, Inc. (NASDAQ:APEI)

author: Robert Leonard
title: American Public Education: Short This Stock As Students Close The Books On Formal Education - American Public Education, Inc. (NASDAQ:APEI)

organizations.name: books on formal education - american public education, inc.

text:
For many decades in the United States, a traditional four-year degree was required to obtain a relatively high-paying corporate job. However, the times and requirements are rapidly changing with the rise of technology. In fact, many of the world’s largest and best-known companies no longer require a college degree for professional positions (product managers, software engineers, senior manager of finance, etc.). This is just the beginning of a major change, and I expect this trend to continue and even accelerate as time goes on. Traditional colleges and universities will certainly feel the increased pressure from this trend, but I believe that for-profit universities such as American Public Education, Inc. ( APEI ) (“American Public”) will feel it even worse. A short position in American Public is recommended because the traditional education system in America is changing, it is facing increased competitive pressures, and it is continually facing heavy regulation.
American Public is a postsecondary education provider through online and on-campus offerings, headquartered in Charles Town, West Virginia, that operates American Military University ("AMU"), American Public University ("APU"), and The Hondros College of Nursing ("HCN").
Source: American Public Education, Inc.
Lead By Millennials, Generation Z Education in the United States Is Transitioning Away From Traditional Degrees Although I am one who has followed the “traditional path” for education, having earned by BBA and MBA degrees from a traditional university, since then I have participated in non-traditional education programs and realized the major benefits they provide. Recently, I wanted to learn how to program, specifically with Python. Rather than spending tens of thousands of dollars on a Computer Science degree from a traditional university, I enrolled in one of the best-selling Python courses on Udemy – Complete Python Bootcamp: Go from zero to hero in Python . I received 24 hours of high-quality content, and it was only $9.99 USD! Now, I understand this course likely did not teach me as much as a Computer Science degree program would, but it did teach me A LOT. It may take 10 of these courses to learn as much as a Computer Science degree program, but at just $100 for 10 courses, the cost isn’t comparable to traditional degree programs.
I had read about many prospective students deciding to forego college, but I didn’t fully understand it until this experience. Not all courses on Udemy are high-quality, but many are, and they provide a strong alternative to traditional education. There are also many other platforms similar to Udemy that provide students with alternative ways of furthering their education and improving their skills. Platforms such as edX, Codeacademy, Udacity, Skillshare, LinkedIn Learning, see the trend towards alternative education taking hold, and they are capitalizing on it. All of these platforms are far more affordable than traditional degree programs, which have increased in cost rapidly over the past 2-3 decades, saving people from adding to the $1.5 trillion student loan debt outstanding in the US. Many prospective students have seen their friends, family, and co-workers going into massive amounts of debt just to get a degree, and they do not want to follow on the same path anymore.
People are realizing that they are still able to obtain the careers they want working at some of their favorite companies, even without a degree. Many major companies, such as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Alphabet ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), IBM ( IBM ), Starbucks ( SBUX ), Whole Foods ( AMZN ), Costco ( COST ), no longer require prospective employees of professional positions (engineers, finance professionals, etc.) to hold four-year degrees, allowing applicants to demonstrate the skills they’ve learned through non-traditional educational sources.
Not only is the cost driving students away, but the alternative education platforms are far more easily accessible and convenient. Students do not have to sit in classrooms for hours on end for four years straight. They are able to login to their computer, from anywhere in the world, complete their assignments and learn their desired skills, much quicker.
According to The National Student Clearinghouse Research Center, total Spring 2017 enrollments are down by 2.4 million from Spring 2011 levels, and more than half a million just from Spring 2015. Even worse, just in the past two years , four-year for-profit universities have seen enrollment drop by more than 224 thousand, or 18%. That’s right, American Public falls within that rapidly declining category, as it is a four-year, for-profit university system company.
Source: Goodcall
Just in the past year, four-year, for-profit universities have seen enrollment fall more than 15%, from just over 901 thousand to 765 thousand.
Source: National Student Clearinghouse Research Center
Why American Public Specifically? Overall, I am quite bearish on the for-profit education sector as whole. However, there are particular headwinds facing American Public that make it an interesting short opportunity.
American Public's total costs and expenses have been rising gradually for the past three years while its revenue has declined. It is also heading into a more capital intensive structure with HCN The majority of its students are full-time active duty military, and It is heavily dependent on government funding - close to receiving too much of its revenue from government sources.
Source: American Public's 10-K
As of the end of 2017, instructional costs and services had gradually increased for three years in a row, and I expect this trend to continue for 2018 and beyond. As of its 3Q2018 10-Q report, for the nine months ended September 30, 2018, instructional costs and services are down slightly, about $670 thousand (but total costs and expenses are still up by about $725 thousand due to the $4 million increase in general and administrative expenses). However, the 4Q is generally its biggest quarter for the instruction costs and services expense, and with the increased faculty from HCN this year I expect 2018 costs to at least meet 2017's, if not exceed. In order to retain and attract top-tier professors, it will need to provide raises and competitive compensation packages, which will increase its costs. Selling and promotion costs were up in 2017 from 2015, and I expect this trend to continue. In American Public's 10-K, they have specifically mentioned having to increase its marketing spend to attract more students.
Acquiring HCN has provided American Public with a reputable nursing program and a larger student body, but due to its in-person, on-campus focus, it is a far more expensive and capital intensive business. I expect American Public to have to increase its CapEx in the coming years to maintain and improve its on-campus facilities. In my opinion, this is the exact opposite direction education providers should be heading. As I've mentioned, trends are pointing towards online and easily-accessible education, yet American Public is investing heavily in expensive on-campus offerings that are losing popularity.
As stated in its 10-K, " As of December 31, 2017 approximately 54% of APUS students self-reported that they served in the military on active duty at the time of initial enrollment. Active duty military students generally take fewer courses per year on average than non-military students. " Given American Public is well-known for being military-focused, I expect it will be hard for it to grow its student body substantially due to the lack of servicemembers' ability to enroll in more courses. Also, given this large military student body, plus additional federal programs, nearly 86% of American Public's revenue comes from the federal government. Although this is not abnormal for for-profit universities, relying so heavily on one source of revenue does pose a major risk to American Public's business. Any change in these programs would provide a material adverse change in American Public's business.
The current, and longest in history, government shutdown also does not bode well for American Public. This is likely a short-term problem that can/will be resolved, but it helps illustrate the problems that can arise from relying so heavily on one major source of revenue.
Source: American Public's 10-K
Education Is A Competitive Space There are few industries that are more competitive than education in the United States. For-profit universities, like American Public, have to compete with non-profit, traditional universities, alternative education providers (as discussed above), and other educational companies like 2U ( TWOU ).
Given that American Public is a for-profit school, it must be thought of like any other business providing a product or service. Is its product/service better than its competitor’s? Can it compete on price? Can it develop, or does it currently have, a competitive advantage? In my opinion, the answers to all of these questions for American Public are NO.
It is difficult, if not impossible, for for-profit universities to provide a higher-quality education (better product/service) than the non-profit universities. The non-profit universities in the United States have been around far longer, have incredible reputations and name brands, and are some of the best schools in the world. Arguably the largest competitive advantage a university can have is its reputation and name. This is an incredibly difficult, and nearly impossible, advantage for American Public to overcome, especially given the inherently poor reputation for-profit universities have garnered over the past few years.
American Public’s programs may be marginally cheaper than some non-profit universities, but certainly not all of them. When considering in-state tuition and many non-profit state schools, a high-quality education can be received for a price quite similar to American Public’s programs. Although American Public could lower its cost in an attempt to drive students to its programs, it is ultimately a business and it cannot discount its products/services too much, just as with any other business. It must maintain a relatively stable price, if not increasing, in order to earn satisfactory margins and profit levels. Regardless of how much it is able to lower the cost of its programs, it will never be able to compete on price with alternative education companies like Udemy. American Public has significant overhead and fixed costs that it must overcome that alternative, online education platforms do not have.
As if for-profit universities weren’t already at a big enough disadvantage, but traditional non-profit education providers are becoming even more competitive by partnering with innovative companies like 2U. Traditional non-profit universities are seeing their enrollment numbers drop and are attempting to become relevant again by providing high-quality, easily-accessible online education through platforms like 2U.
For-Profit Universities Are Notoriously Regulated I am not going to spend significant time covering this topic, as it is a popular topic for news outlets and debate amongst politicians. It has also been well-written about, on both sides, on Seeking Alpha by Duane Bair , Larry Ramer , and others. I did want to at least briefly mention it as it is a major risk facing for-profit university companies such as American Public. With a significant portion of American Public’s revenues coming from the federal government, it is highly dependent upon government funding for educational programs. The amount of funding available for programs American Public depends on for its revenue ebbs and flows with who is in office. President Obama was more “strict” on for-profit universities funding and regulation, while President Trump tends to be more lenient. There is no way of knowing what future presidents' actions will be towards for-profit education companies, but as long as American Public continues to receive more than 80% of its revenue from government-funded programs, it will be a major risk facing American Public’s business.
Shortability and Its Risks According to Interactive Brokers, as of this writing there were about 1.5 million shares available to short. The availability of shares available to short does fluctuate from time to time, but in general, there are plenty of shares available to short for investors interested in doing so.
Source: Interactive Brokers
The risks to a short position in American Public’s stock are the inherent risks of shorting stocks, an acquisition of another education company, being acquired itself, enrollment increasing, alternative education partnership, or government funding significantly increasing.
Shorting stocks has the inherent risk of unlimited loss with a maximum gain of 100%. Similar to its acquisition of The Hondros College of Nursing, American Public could acquire another smaller education institution to broaden its reach, increase its enrollment and improve its recognition. Given that American Public is not a massive company, with a market cap of just about $500 million, it is possible that a larger education company could purchase American Public at a premium to today’s price, providing a loss to short investors. It is also possible that the trend toward alternative education fades, resulting in traditional education enrollment rising. American Public’s increased marketing efforts could also result in increased enrollment numbers, and therefore increased revenue.
Short investors also face the risk of American Public improving its operating results by partnering with an innovative education company like 2U. Although 2U is not focused on profits currently, if this changes in the future, it could increase enrollment in online programs at American Public, resulting in higher revenue, and unleashing significant value. There is also the potential that a platform similar to 2U, but not 2U itself, will be created and tailored to for-profit education companies. Any partnership between American Public and 2U (or similar company) would likely unleash great value and threaten a short position. Changes within the federal government that are in favor of for-profit institutions and increased funding for government-funded educational programs would present a significant risk for short investors as well.
Financials and Valuation Since reaching all-time high revenue of $350 million in 2014, revenues have decreased by over $50 million, or about 15%, and net income has been cut in half or about 50%. Over the past five years, gross margins have slowly contracted from a high of 66% to just over 61%, with operating margins dropping from 21% to 12% and net margins from 13% to 8%. Over the past ten years, American Public has bought back about 3 million shares of stock, but has been slowly increasing its share counts as of late.
As of the third quarter of 2018, American Public had a relatively healthy balance sheet. It has about $197 million in cash and $358 million in total assets, with only about $48 million in total liabilities. It has also consistently generated positive cash flow, averaging about $35 million per year over the past five years.
I expect American Public’s revenue, profits, and margins to continue to fall, given the risks the company is facing, as discussed above. Given that students are generally enrolled in multi-year programs, I do not expect revenues to fall precipitously next year, or even the year after, but I do expect new enrollment figures to decline, and ultimately revenue pullback. I also expect that American Public will have to increase its SG&A and salary expenses, which will reduce its profits.
Source: Data, Morningstar ; Table, Self-created
Given the headwinds I expect American Public to face in the coming years, I believe it will not live up to its current valuation, and is overvalued on a discounted cash flow and multiple basis. Assuming American Public will grow its free cash flow 5% annually over the next five years, and 2% annually over the following five years, at discount rate of 12% and a TV multiple of 6x, I value American Public’s stock at about $18-19 per share –36% below today’s levels. That is assuming rather optimistic growth figures; more realistically, I expect its cash flow to grow at about 2% over the next five years, and 0-1% over the following five years. Using the same discount rate and TV multiple as previously mentioned, this values the stock closer to $16-17 per share.
Source: Data, Morningstar ; Table, Self-created.
Based on the financial projections and expected P/E multiples above, my calculations point to a fair value of $16-18 for the stock by the end of 2019, and down to a fair value of about $7.30-9 by the end of 2020. However, if the risks discussed above in the “ Shortability and Its Risks ” section were to materialize, I see potential upside risk in the $33-39 range.
Source: Data, Morningstar ; Table, Self-created.
The Bottom Line American Public operates in a heavily regulated industry that has claimed multiple victims over the past few years ( Education Corporation of America , ITT Educational Services , and Corinthian Colleges ). Although I do not expect American Public to fold in the way these three companies have, I do expect it to face strong headwinds going forward, providing an interesting short opportunity for investors.
The trend of people turning to alternative education platforms is really just beginning, and for-profit universities are already seeing enrollment drop significantly. As more companies begin to hire new employees without requiring a four-year degree, low-cost education solutions are created, and student loan debt remains a major issue, for-profit universities will continue to see declining enrollment. Declining enrollment is a tall task for American Public to attempt to correct. I expect their increased marketing efforts will fail to reverse the declining enrollment and its future financial results will suffer.
